hints: Start from the parent chain but-1-ene with the double bond at carbon 1, then add a methyl branch on carbon 2 and count the carbons.
walkthrough:
Build the carbon backbone in your head**
Picture but-1-ene first. That is a four carbon chain with a double bond right at the start: $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Now add the 2-methyl part, which means an extra $\text{CH}_3$ joined to carbon 2. So you get $\text{CH}_2=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

Convert to skeletal lines**
In skeletal, each bend and end is a carbon and you do not draw C-H bonds. Draw a double line for $\text{C1=C2}$, then a short branch up or down from C2 for the methyl group, then two more single lines for C3 and C4. The double bond must stay at the end of the chain.
Final answer: Skeletal formula showing $\text{CH}_2=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, a C=C at the end with a branch on the second carbon.

hints: Recall the two different sets of conditions for $\text{MnO}_4^-$ with an alkene, mild to make a diol versus vigorous to break the double bond completely.
walkthrough:
Link conditions to how far oxidation goes**
Cold, dilute acidified manganate(VII) only adds OH groups across the double bond to give a diol. To actually split the $\text{C=C}$ into two carbonyl fragments as shown here, you need much more vigorous oxidation.

State the vigorous pair**
That vigorous set is heat plus concentrated reagent. So the specific conditions are hot and concentrated acidified manganate(VII) ions.
Final answer: Hot and concentrated acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$.

hints: Think about what happens to the organic molecule when it gains oxygen atoms from $\text{MnO}_4^-$ and the manganate ion itself is reduced.
walkthrough:
See it from the organic side**
The alkene gains oxygen atoms to become carbonyl compounds $\text{X}$ and $\text{Y}$. Gain of oxygen, or loss of hydrogen, is oxidation. The purple $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is the oxidising agent and is itself reduced.
Final answer: Oxidation.

hints: Split the $\text{C=C}$ of $\text{CH}_2=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ into two fragments and remember the $\text{CH}_2=$ end first becomes methanoic acid before further oxidation.
walkthrough:
Split the double bond**
Cut $\text{CH}_2=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ at the $\text{C=C}$. The left $\text{CH}_2=$ fragment picks up O to give $\text{HCHO}$ then $\text{HCOOH}$. The right fragment gives the ketone $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3$ which is Y.

Explain why X goes further**
Methanoic acid still has an aldehyde-like H attached to the $\text{C=O}$, so hot concentrated $\text{MnO}_4^-$ oxidises it straight on to $\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. That is why the scheme shows X as the intermediate that immediately forms $\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. So X is $\text{HCOOH}$.
Final answer: $\text{HCOOH}$ or $\text{HCO}_2\text{H}$, methanoic acid.

hints: Recall the specific reagent that gives a coloured solid with both aldehydes and ketones but not with other functional groups.
Remember the characteristic colour range of the hydrazone precipitate formed in this test.
walkthrough:
Choose the carbonyl reagent**
Y is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3$, a ketone. The classic identification reagent for the $\text{C=O}$ group in aldehydes and ketones is 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine, often called 2,4-DNPH or Brady's reagent. Add a small amount of Y to the DNPH solution.

Record the positive sign**
A positive result is not a colour change in solution but formation of a bright solid. You see a yellow, orange or red precipitate of the 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone. That confirms the carbonyl group.
Final answer: Add 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH); yellow / orange / red precipitate forms.

hints: Compare the bonds present: 2-methylbut-1-ene has $\text{=C-H}$ and $\text{C=C}$ while Y has only alkyl $\text{C-H}$ and $\text{C=O}$, and focus only above $1500 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.
Recall the approximate positions: $\text{=C-H}$ just above $3000 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, $\text{C=C}$ near $1650 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, and ketone $\text{C=O}$ between $1670$ and $1740 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Spot the loss of the alkene C-H**
Look above $3000 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. 2-methylbut-1-ene shows a sharp dip just above $3000 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, about $3100 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, due to the $\text{=C-H}$ stretch. Y, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3$, has only saturated alkyl $\text{C-H}$ below $3000 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, so that $3100 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ peak disappears.

Swap C=C for C=O**
Now look near $1650 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. The alkene shows $\text{C=C}$ stretching there. In Y there is no $\text{C=C}$, so that peak is gone. Instead Y contains a ketone $\text{C=O}$, which absorbs more strongly and slightly to the left, anywhere in the range $1670$ to $1740 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. That appearance of a $\text{C=O}$ peak plus loss of the $\text{C=C}$ peak is the second main difference.

Final answer: Absence of absorption near $3100 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ in Y as no $\text{=C-H}$ present; peak at $1650 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ for $\text{C=C}$ absent in Y and new peak between $1670$-$1740 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ in Y due to $\text{C=O}$.

hints: Remember that $\text{LiAlH}_4$ reduces a carboxylic acid all the way to a primary alcohol by adding four $[\text{H}]$ and producing water as the second product.
walkthrough:
Balance the reduction with [H]**
Think of $[\text{H}]$ as a hydrogen atom supplied by $\text{LiAlH}_4$. Propanoic acid $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ needs four $[\text{H}]$ to convert the $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ group into $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$. The extra O leaves as $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. So write $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H} + 4[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ and check atoms balance.

hints: Name the three carbon alcohol with the OH on the end carbon formed from propanoic acid.
walkthrough:
Name the three carbon chain**
The product $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ has three carbons with OH on carbon 1. That is propan-1-ol, a primary alcohol.
Final answer: Propan-1-ol.

hints: Work out the molecular formula of propanoic acid $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ first, since an isomer must have exactly the same atoms.
walkthrough:
Count atoms in propanoic acid**
$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ contains 3 carbons, 6 hydrogens and 2 oxygens. A structural isomer has the same molecular formula with atoms joined differently, so W is also $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$.

hints: Rearrange the $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$ atoms into an ester $\text{RCOOR'}$ by splitting the carbons between the acid part and the alcohol part.
walkthrough:
Fit three carbons into an ester**
An ester needs $\text{-COO-}$ in the middle. With only three carbons total you have two options. Put two carbons in the acid part and one in the alcohol part to get methyl ethanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_3$. Or put one carbon in the acid part and two in the alcohol part to get ethyl methanoate, $\text{HCOOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Either structure is a correct ester isomer of propanoic acid.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_3$ or $\text{HCOOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$.
